name: Bits → bytes
description: Converts a number of bits to bytes by dividing by 8, since one byte contains eight bits. It expresses data volume in the larger byte unit.
notes: This is the standard 8 bits per byte. Note that storage sizes use bytes while transmission rates are often quoted in bits, so the two differ by a factor of 8.

name: Gibibytes → bytes
description: Converts gibibytes to bytes by multiplying by 1024 cubed (1,073,741,824). Gibibytes are the binary-based unit, distinct from decimal gigabytes.
notes: A gibibyte (GiB) uses 1024³ bytes, while a gigabyte (GB) is 1000³ bytes; the two differ by about 7%. Use this for binary GiB, not decimal GB.

name: Mbps → MB/s
description: Converts a bit rate in megabits per second to megabytes per second by dividing by 8. It shows how fast data transfers in byte terms from a bit-based speed.
notes: Divides by 8 bits per byte; this mixes decimal-megabit rates with megabytes, so it is the common networking convention rather than binary MiB. A 100 Mbps link is about 12.5 MB/s.

name: File transfer time
description: Estimates the time to transfer a file as its size in megabytes times 8, divided by the link speed in megabits per second. The factor of 8 converts bytes to bits so units match.
notes: Size is in megabytes and speed in megabits per second, giving seconds. This is an ideal estimate that ignores protocol overhead, latency, and real-world throughput loss.

name: Bit rate
description: Computes the bit rate as the amount of data in bits divided by the transfer duration, giving bits per second. It measures how quickly data flows over time.
notes: Data size must be in bits and duration in seconds to get bits per second. If your data is in bytes, multiply by 8 first.

name: Megapixels
description: Computes an image sensor's resolution in megapixels as width times height in pixels, divided by one million. It gives the total pixel count in millions.
notes: Width and height are in pixels; the result is the total, not a linear dimension. Effective (recorded) megapixels can be slightly below the sensor's nominal count.

name: Aspect ratio
description: Computes the aspect ratio of an image or screen as its width divided by its height. A value of about 1.778 corresponds to the common 16:9 widescreen format.
notes: Width and height must use the same unit so the ratio is dimensionless. The result is a decimal ratio; convert to a form like 16:9 separately if needed.

name: Pixel density (DPI)
description: Computes a display's pixel density in dots per inch as the diagonal pixel count (hypotenuse of width and height) divided by the diagonal size in inches. Higher DPI means a sharper, finer image.
notes: Width and height are in pixels and diagonal in inches; hypot gives the diagonal pixel length. Higher DPI on a screen means finer detail, unlike loosely used print DPI.

name: Decibel gain (voltage)
description: Computes voltage gain in decibels as 20 times the base-10 logarithm of the output-to-input voltage ratio. Each 20 dB corresponds to a tenfold change in voltage.
notes: The factor is 20 for voltage (amplitude) ratios; power ratios use 10 instead. A negative result means attenuation, and the ratio must be positive.

name: Shannon channel capacity
description: Computes the Shannon-Hartley maximum error-free data rate of a channel as bandwidth times the base-2 logarithm of one plus the signal-to-noise ratio. It sets the theoretical upper limit on reliable throughput.
notes: SNR is entered as a linear power ratio, not in decibels. Bandwidth is in hertz and the result in bits per second is a theoretical ceiling, unreachable in practice.

name: Nyquist Sampling Rate
description: Gives the minimum sampling rate for a signal as twice its maximum frequency, the Nyquist rate. Sampling at or above this rate lets the original signal be reconstructed without aliasing.
notes: This is a theoretical minimum; real systems sample somewhat higher and add an anti-aliasing filter. The signal must be band-limited to fmax for the rule to hold.

name: Nyquist Maximum Data Rate
description: Gives the maximum data rate of a noiseless channel as 2×B×log2(M), from bandwidth B and the number of discrete signal levels M. More levels or wider bandwidth carry more bits per second.
notes: Applies to an ideal noiseless channel; with noise, use the Shannon capacity instead. M is the number of signal levels, so each symbol carries log2(M) bits.

name: Channel Capacity (SNR ratio)
description: The Shannon–Hartley theorem gives the maximum error-free capacity of a noisy channel as B×log2(1+SNR), from bandwidth B and the signal-to-noise ratio. It is the upper limit on reliable data rate.
notes: SNR is a linear power ratio here, not decibels; convert dB with 10^(dB/10) first. This is a theoretical ceiling that real coding schemes only approach.

name: Bandwidth-Delay Product
description: Gives the bandwidth-delay product as bandwidth times round-trip time, the number of bits in transit on the link at once. It sets the buffer or window size needed to keep a link fully utilised.
notes: Bandwidth in bits per second and RTT in seconds give the result in bits; divide by 8 for bytes. A TCP window smaller than this value limits throughput below the link's capacity.

name: Usable Hosts per Subnet
description: Gives the number of usable host addresses in a subnet as 2^h − 2, from the number of host bits h. The subtraction removes the reserved network and broadcast addresses.
notes: The −2 accounts for the network and broadcast addresses; with 0 or 1 host bits the classic formula yields none. IPv6 and some point-to-point cases do not reserve these two.

name: Number of Subnets
description: Gives the number of equal-size subnets created when you borrow n bits from the host portion of an address. Each borrowed bit doubles the count, so the total is 2 raised to the power n.
notes: n is the number of subnet bits borrowed, not the prefix length. Some older schemes reserve the all-zeros and all-ones subnets, reducing the usable count.

name: IPv4 Addresses in Prefix
description: Counts the total IPv4 addresses contained in a block with the given prefix length p. Since IPv4 has 32 bits, the host portion is 32 minus p bits, giving 2 to the power of that as the address count.
notes: This is the raw total; in a normal subnet the network and broadcast addresses are not assignable to hosts, so usable hosts are two fewer (except for /31 and /32).

name: Throughput
description: Computes the average data transfer rate by dividing the amount of data moved by the time it took. The result is expressed in bits per second.
notes: Keep data in bits and time in seconds for bps; if data is in bytes, multiply by 8 first. This is an average rate, not the instantaneous peak.

name: Propagation Delay
description: Gives the time a signal takes to travel a link, found by dividing the link distance by the propagation speed of the signal in the medium. The result is in seconds.
notes: This is only propagation delay, not transmission, queuing, or processing delay. Propagation speed in cables is typically 0.6 to 0.7 times the speed of light in vacuum.

name: Audio Bit Rate (PCM)
description: Calculates the raw bit rate of uncompressed PCM audio by multiplying the sample rate, the bit depth per sample, and the number of channels. The result is in bits per second.
notes: This applies to uncompressed PCM only; compressed formats like MP3 or AAC use far lower rates. Multiply by duration to estimate file size in bits.

name: Uncompressed Video Bit Rate
description: Estimates the bit rate of raw uncompressed video by multiplying the frame width and height in pixels by the frame rate and the color depth per pixel. The result is in bits per second.
notes: This is the uncompressed rate; real codecs such as H.264 or H.265 reduce it by orders of magnitude. Color depth here is total bits per pixel across all channels.

name: File Size from Bit Rate
description: Gives the size of a media file by multiplying its bit rate by its duration. With bit rate in bits per second and duration in seconds, the result is the total size in bits.
notes: Divide by 8 for bytes, and by 8 million for megabytes. This assumes a constant bit rate; variable-bit-rate streams give only an approximate size.

name: Compression Ratio
description: Expresses how much a file was compressed as the ratio of the original size to the compressed size. A value of 4 means the original is four times larger than the compressed version.
notes: Both sizes must use the same unit. This is a ratio, not a percentage; for the fraction of space saved use a separate space-saving formula.

name: Space Saving
description: Gives the fraction of storage saved by compression, computed as one minus the compressed size divided by the original size. A result of 0.75 means 75 percent of the space was saved.
notes: Result is a fraction from 0 to 1; multiply by 100 for a percentage. Both sizes must share the same unit, and the compressed size should not exceed the original.

name: Total Pixels
description: Counts the total number of pixels in an image or display by multiplying its width by its height in pixels. For example 1920 by 1080 gives about 2.07 million pixels.
notes: This counts pixel positions, not memory; storage also depends on bits per pixel. Divide by one million for megapixels.

name: Pixels Per Inch (PPI)
description: Computes a display's pixel density by dividing the diagonal resolution in pixels, found from the Pythagorean combination of width and height pixels, by the physical diagonal size in inches.
notes: The diagonal size must be in inches; higher PPI means finer detail. It assumes square pixels and a screen whose pixel aspect ratio matches its physical shape.

name: Dot Pitch
description: Gives the spacing between adjacent pixel centers in millimeters by dividing 25.4, the number of millimeters in an inch, by the pixel density in pixels per inch. Higher density gives a smaller dot pitch.
notes: The constant 25.4 fixes the unit to millimeters per pixel. Dot pitch is the inverse of PPI, so denser displays have finer pitch.

name: RAID 5 Usable Capacity
description: Gives the usable storage of a RAID 5 array as the number of drives minus one, multiplied by the capacity of a single drive. One drive's worth of space is consumed by distributed parity.
notes: Assumes all drives are the same size; a mixed array is limited by the smallest drive. RAID 5 tolerates the failure of one drive only.

name: RAID 6 Usable Capacity
description: Gives the usable storage of a RAID 6 array as the number of drives minus two, multiplied by the capacity of a single drive. Two drives' worth of space is used for dual parity.
notes: Assumes uniform drive sizes; a mixed array is capped by the smallest drive. RAID 6 tolerates the simultaneous failure of any two drives.

name: RAID 10 Usable Capacity
description: Gives the usable storage of a RAID 10 array as half the number of drives multiplied by the capacity of a single drive, since every drive is mirrored by a partner.
notes: Requires an even number of same-size drives. It survives multiple drive failures only if no complete mirror pair is lost at once.

name: Error-Correction Capability
description: Gives how many bit errors a block code can correct, as the floor of the minimum Hamming distance minus one, divided by two. A code with minimum distance 5 can correct up to two errors.
notes: dmin is the minimum Hamming distance between valid codewords. The result is a whole number of correctable errors; detection capability is higher than correction.

name: Self-Information
description: Gives the information content, or surprise, of a single event in bits as the negative base-2 logarithm of its probability. Rarer events carry more information.
notes: p must be strictly between 0 and 1; a probability of 1 gives zero information. Enter p as a fraction, not a percentage.

name: Hash Table Load Factor
description: Gives a hash table's load factor as the number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets. It measures how full the table is and predicts collision likelihood.
notes: For open addressing the load factor stays at or below 1; for chaining it can exceed 1. Higher load factors slow lookups, so tables are often resized near a threshold.

name: Exponential Complexity O(2^n)
description: Gives the number of basic operations for an algorithm with exponential time complexity of order 2 to the n, where n is the input size. The count doubles with each additional unit of input.
notes: This is an asymptotic order-of-growth estimate, not an exact operation count. Even modest n values become computationally infeasible very quickly.

name: Cache Hit Ratio
description: Gives the fraction of memory accesses served from cache, as the number of hits divided by the total of hits plus misses. A value near 1 means the cache is very effective.
notes: Hits and misses must be counts over the same period. The hit ratio and miss ratio always sum to 1; multiply by 100 for a percentage.

name: Cache Miss Ratio
description: Gives the fraction of memory accesses not found in cache, as the number of misses divided by the total of hits plus misses. A lower value indicates better cache performance.
notes: Counts must cover the same interval. The miss ratio equals one minus the hit ratio; multiply by 100 for a percentage.

name: Cycles Per Instruction (CPI)
description: Gives the average number of clock cycles a processor spends per instruction, as total clock cycles divided by total instructions executed. Lower CPI means higher efficiency per instruction.
notes: This is an average over a workload; individual instructions vary widely in cycle cost. CPI is the reciprocal of instructions per cycle (IPC).

name: MIPS Rate
description: Gives a processor's rate in millions of instructions per second, as the clock frequency divided by the cycles per instruction and by one million. It combines clock speed and efficiency into a throughput figure.
notes: Enter frequency in hertz. MIPS depends on the instruction mix, so it is unreliable for comparing different instruction-set architectures.

name: Amdahl's Speedup
description: Gives the overall speedup from parallelizing a program, where p is the parallelizable fraction sped up by a factor s. The serial part 1 minus p limits the achievable gain.
notes: Enter p as a fraction from 0 to 1. Speedup is capped by the serial portion, so improving s eventually yields diminishing returns.

name: Amdahl Maximum Speedup
description: Gives the theoretical upper limit on speedup under Amdahl's law when the parallel part is infinitely fast, as one divided by the serial fraction 1 minus p. This is the ceiling no amount of parallelism can exceed.
notes: Enter p as a fraction; only the serial fraction matters here. For example a 90 percent parallel program can never exceed a 10x speedup.

name: Gustafson Scaled Speedup
description: Gives the scaled speedup under Gustafson's law for n processors when the serial fraction is s, as n minus n minus one times s. It models keeping run time fixed while enlarging the problem.
notes: Enter s as a fraction of the work that stays serial. Unlike Amdahl's law it assumes the workload grows with the processor count, so speedup scales more optimistically.

name: Clock Period
description: Gives the duration of one clock cycle as the reciprocal of the clock frequency. A 3 GHz clock, for instance, has a period of about 0.33 nanoseconds.
notes: Enter frequency in hertz to get the period in seconds. The clock period is the inverse of frequency, so faster clocks have shorter periods.

name: Memory Address Space
description: Gives the number of distinct addresses an address bus can reference, as 2 raised to the width of the bus in bits. A 32-bit bus can address about 4.29 billion locations.
notes: This counts addressable units, usually bytes, not total capacity in bits. A 32-bit address space corresponds to 4 GiB when each address is one byte.

name: Representable Colors
description: Gives the total number of distinct colors that can be represented at a given color depth, as 2 raised to the number of bits. A 24-bit depth yields about 16.7 million colors.
notes: For per-channel RGB the total bits are the sum across channels, so 8 bits each gives 24-bit color. An alpha channel adds transparency levels, not colors.

name: RGB Relative Luminance
description: Estimates the perceived brightness of an RGB color as a weighted sum of its red, green, and blue channels, using coefficients 0.2126, 0.7152, and 0.0722. Green contributes most to perceived luminance.
notes: These Rec. 709 weights assume linear (gamma-decoded) channel values; applying them to raw sRGB values gives only an approximation. Result scales with the channel range used.

name: Two-Digit Hex to Decimal
description: Converts a two-digit hexadecimal number to decimal by multiplying the high digit's value by 16 and adding the low digit's value. For example FF gives 255.
notes: Each digit value must be between 0 and 15, where A through F correspond to 10 through 15. The result ranges from 0 to 255, matching one byte.

name: Goodput (with loss)
description: Gives the effective useful throughput, or goodput, as the raw bandwidth multiplied by the fraction of data that is not lost, that is one minus the loss fraction. It reflects data actually delivered.
notes: Enter loss as a fraction from 0 to 1, not a percentage. This simple model accounts only for loss, not protocol overhead or retransmission timing.

name: Bit Error Rate (BER)
description: Gives the bit error rate as the number of bits received in error divided by the total number of bits transmitted. It measures the reliability of a digital transmission link.
notes: Both counts must be over the same transmission. BER is a dimensionless ratio, often extremely small and written in scientific notation such as 5e-6.

name: Packets Needed
description: Gives the number of packets required to carry a payload, as the total payload size divided by the payload capacity per packet, rounded up. Any leftover data needs one more full packet.
notes: The ceiling accounts for a final partial packet. mtu here is usable payload per packet, not the full frame including headers, so use the correct value.

name: CPU Execution Time
description: Gives the time a CPU takes to run a program, as the instruction count multiplied by the cycles per instruction and divided by the clock frequency. It links the three classic performance factors.
notes: Enter frequency in hertz to get time in seconds. This is the CPU time only, excluding waiting on I/O or memory stalls beyond what CPI captures.

name: Effective Memory Access Time
description: Gives the average memory access time as a weighted blend of cache and main-memory times: the hit rate times the cache access time plus the miss rate times the memory access time. Misses dominate the average unless the hit rate is very high.
notes: Enter the hit rate as a fraction from 0 to 1; the miss rate is one minus it. A simple two-level model that ignores miss penalties like page faults.

name: Symbol Rate (Baud)
description: Gives the symbol rate in baud as the bit rate divided by the number of bits carried per symbol. When each symbol carries more than one bit, the baud rate is lower than the bit rate.
notes: Baud counts symbols per second, not bits per second; the two are equal only when each symbol carries one bit. Higher-order modulation packs more bits per symbol.

name: Frame Period
description: Gives the time between successive frames as the reciprocal of the frame rate. At 60 frames per second, for example, each frame lasts about 16.7 milliseconds.
notes: Enter the frame rate in frames per second to get the period in seconds. The frame period is the inverse of frame rate, so higher rates give shorter frame times.

name: Contrast Ratio
description: Gives a display's contrast ratio as the maximum luminance divided by the minimum luminance. A result of 500 is written as 500:1 and indicates how distinct the brightest and darkest tones are.
notes: Both luminances must use the same unit, and the minimum must be greater than zero. Measurement conditions strongly affect the value, so quoted ratios vary widely.

name: Little's Law (Items in System)
description: Gives the average number of items in a stable system as the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends in the system. It holds regardless of the arrival or service distribution.
notes: The rates and times must use consistent units, and the system must be in steady state. It counts items being served plus those waiting.

name: Server Utilization
description: Gives a single server's utilization, or traffic intensity, as the arrival rate divided by the service rate. A value of 0.8 means the server is busy 80 percent of the time.
notes: Arrival and service rates must use the same time unit. For a stable single-server queue this ratio must stay below 1, or the queue grows without bound.

name: M/M/1 Average Number in System
description: Gives the average number of customers in an M/M/1 queue as the traffic intensity rho divided by one minus rho. As rho approaches 1, the average number grows without bound.
notes: Valid only for a stable queue where rho is below 1. It assumes Poisson arrivals, exponential service times, and a single server.

name: Disk Capacity (CHS)
description: Gives a disk's raw capacity in bytes from its cylinder-head-sector geometry, by multiplying the number of cylinders, heads, sectors per track, and bytes per sector together.
notes: This gives raw geometric capacity; usable space is less after formatting. Modern drives use logical block addressing, so reported CHS values are often virtual rather than physical.

name: Nibbles in Data
description: Gives the number of nibbles in a block of data by dividing the number of bits by four, since one nibble is four bits. A nibble corresponds to a single hexadecimal digit.
notes: The bit count should be a multiple of 4 for a whole number of nibbles. Two nibbles make one byte, so nibbles are half the byte count.
